planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; established clumps spread steadily by rhizome and are easily lifted and divided every few years.

directions: Superba is a vigorous selection of clustered bellflower prized for its extra-large, densely packed heads of rich violet-purple bells, noticeably bolder in both flower size and color saturation than the straight species. Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in average, well-drained soil, where it spreads by rhizome to form a substantial, long-lived patch. Deadhead the main flower clusters after the first flush to tidy the planting and coax a lighter rebloom later in summer. Because it spreads readily, give it room among other vigorous perennials or plan to divide it every few years to keep it in bounds.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Telham Beauty Peach-Leaved Bellflower (Large China-Blue Cup Flowers)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring into well-drained, average garden soil; Telham Beauty prefers cooler summers and benefits from afternoon shade and reliable moisture in hot climates, same as the species.

directions: Telham Beauty is a long-favored heirloom selection of peach-leaved bellflower, distinguished by unusually large, saucer-shaped, china-blue flowers held wide open on slender, wiry stems above narrow, willow-like foliage. The oversized blooms make it an outstanding cut flower and a showstopper in the early to midsummer border. Grow it in well-drained soil with some afternoon shade in warm climates, and divide congested clumps every few years in early spring or fall to maintain vigor, since it can be somewhat short-lived without periodic renewal. Deadheading spent stems often coaxes a second, lighter flush of bloom.

common_name: Blue Clips Tussock Bellflower (Compact Award-Winning Blue Cups)

planting.note: Surface-sow; seed needs light to germinate. Often blooms the first year if started early indoors, and reliably by the second year from direct-sown seed.

directions: Blue Clips is a long-popular, award-winning selection of tussock bellflower valued for its exceptionally neat, dense mounding habit and abundant crop of upward-facing, cup-shaped violet-blue flowers produced over a long summer season. It stays lower and more compact than typical seed strains of the species, making it especially well suited to rock gardens, container edges, and the front of a border. Grow in full sun to part shade in cool, well-drained soil, and shear the plant back lightly after the first flush of bloom to tidy the mound and encourage repeat flowering. It is reliably perennial and needs little care once established.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Surface-sow seed in spring or plant container-grown divisions into well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun to part shade; good drainage is essential, especially over winter.

directions: Adriatic bellflower is a low, trailing rock-garden species native to limestone cliffs of the Balkan coast, forming a loose mat of small, heart-shaped leaves studded in early to midsummer with abundant star-shaped, lavender-blue flowers with a distinct pale center. Its cascading habit makes it well suited to tumbling over rock walls, spilling from containers, and filling gaps between paving stones, much like its taller relative C. poscharskyana but in a smaller, tidier scale. Plant in lean, well-drained soil, since rich soil or excess moisture encourages rot and floppy growth. Shear lightly after the main bloom flush to keep the mat compact and to encourage sporadic rebloom into fall.

planting.note: Sow seed in spring or plant divisions into moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; spreads by rhizome, so site where its wandering habit is welcome or plan to divide and contain it periodically.

directions: Korean bellflower, native to Ulleungdo Island off the Korean coast, produces large, pendant, bell-shaped flowers in pale pink to white, generously speckled with maroon spots inside the throat, carried above glossy, heart-shaped foliage from early to midsummer. It is notably more shade-tolerant than most bellflowers, thriving in dappled woodland-edge light where many campanulas struggle, and it spreads by rhizome to form an expanding colony over time — vigorous enough that it works best in informal beds or naturalized areas rather than tightly controlled borders. Divide congested clumps in spring or fall to refresh vigor and manage its spread. Deer- and rabbit-resistant, and largely untroubled by pests.

planting.note: Plant small divisions or container-grown plants in spring into gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun to part shade; established mats spread readily by thin creeping rhizomes and are simple to divide.

directions: Fairy thimbles is a diminutive alpine bellflower native to the mountains of central and southern Europe, forming a low, creeping mat of tiny rounded leaves from which wiry, thread-thin stems rise to just a few inches, each nodding with small, pale blue-violet, thimble-shaped bells in early to midsummer. Its miniature scale and cheerfully thuggish spreading habit make it a favorite for rock garden crevices, trough gardens, and gaps between paving, where it seeds and creeps into an ever-widening carpet without overwhelming larger neighbors. Sharp drainage is essential, particularly through winter, as the shallow roots rot readily in heavy or waterlogged soil. Established colonies are extremely low-maintenance and rarely need dividing except to control spread.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Sarastro Bellflower (Extra-Large Deep Violet Pendant Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Sarastro tolerates more shade than most bellflower hybrids and appreciates protection from hot afternoon sun in warm climates.

directions: Sarastro is a robust hybrid bellflower bred for exceptionally large, deep violet-purple pendant bells, each up to three inches long and held in graceful profusion along arching stems well above the clumping, glossy foliage. It blooms over an unusually long season from early summer into fall, especially if spent flower stems are cut back after the first flush. Unlike some vigorously spreading bellflower species, Sarastro forms a well-behaved, expanding clump rather than running aggressively by rhizome, making it easier to place in a mixed border. It tolerates a good measure of shade for a bellflower, performing well at a woodland edge or under high, dappled canopy.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for winter-spring germination, or plant container divisions in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Western blue-eyed grass follows California's winter-wet, summer-dry rainfall pattern and often goes summer-dormant without irrigation.

directions: Western blue-eyed grass is a California native member of the iris family, forming neat clumps of flat, grass-like foliage topped in spring with cheerful, six-petaled, violet-blue flowers with a bright yellow center. It follows the region's Mediterranean rainfall pattern, growing actively and flowering through the cool, wet winter and spring before going dormant or semi-dormant through the dry summer heat, especially without supplemental water. Excellent in meadow plantings, native grasslands, and rock gardens, where it self-sows modestly to form soft colonies over time. Little care is needed beyond cutting back dried summer foliage, and established clumps are quite drought-tolerant.

common_name: Quaint and Queerly Blue-Eyed Grass (Bicolor Blue-and-White Flowers)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring into moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; divide and replant regularly to maintain the distinctive bicolor flower pattern, since seedlings can revert to solid blue.

directions: Quaint and Queerly is an old heirloom selection of blue-eyed grass prized for its curious, two-toned flowers, each petal split cleanly between violet-blue and white to give the tiny six-petaled blooms an unusual pinwheel patchwork effect. In every other respect it shares the charming, grass-like foliage and cheerful, prolific late-spring-through-summer flowering of the species. Because the distinctive bicolor pattern does not always come true from self-sown seedlings, propagate named divisions to maintain the true form. Grow in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, and use it the same way as the species — at the front of a border, in rock gardens, or along stream banks.
